min-stack.statement: Support push, pop, top, and getMin. Assume pop, top, and getMin receive a nonempty stack.
min-stack.example: push(3), push(1), push(1), pop() → minimum remains 1.
hints: Store minimum information alongside ordinary values.
Duplicate minima must survive until their final occurrence is removed.

approaches.name: Scan on demand
approaches.explanation: Keep values in an ArrayList. Scan all current values when asked for the minimum.
approaches.tradeoff: Simple storage, but repeated minimum queries are expensive.

approaches.name: Minimum at every depth
approaches.explanation: Each entry stores its value and the minimum at its depth. Popping automatically restores the previous minimum.
approaches.tradeoff: One extra integer per entry buys constant-time minimum queries.

min-stack.followup: How would you add getMax? Why does one global minimum fail after a pop?

implement-queue-using-stacks.statement: Implement FIFO push, pop, peek, and empty using stacks. Pop and peek receive a nonempty queue.
hints: One stack reverses order. Two reversals restore FIFO order.
Transfer input elements only when the output stack is empty.

approaches.name: Lazy two-stack queue
approaches.explanation: Push into the input stack. If output is empty, transfer all input values to output. Every value moves at most once.
approaches.tradeoff: Efficient total throughput, but transferring creates a latency spike for a single operation. An eager version can instead make push O(n) and pop O(1).

implement-queue-using-stacks.followup: Explain amortized versus worst-case complexity. Why must transfer wait until output is empty?

search-in-rotated-sorted-array.statement: Return the target index in a rotated ascending array of distinct integers, or -1.
hints: At least one side of the midpoint is sorted.
Check whether the target lies within that sorted half before discarding it.

approaches.name: Linear scan
approaches.explanation: Compare the target against each element.
approaches.tradeoff: Works with duplicates too, but ignores the ordering.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int search(int[] a,int t){for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)if(a[i]==t)return i;return -1;}}

approaches.name: Modified binary search
approaches.explanation: Keep an inclusive candidate interval. Identify the sorted half and retain it only if its value range contains the target.
approaches.tradeoff: The logarithmic guarantee assumes distinct values. Duplicate values can make the sorted half ambiguous.

search-in-rotated-sorted-array.followup: Trace an unrotated array and a one-element array. How would duplicates change the algorithm?

search-a-2d-matrix.statement: Search a rectangular matrix ordered globally when read row by row. Each row begins after the previous row ends.
hints: Treat the matrix as a virtual sorted array.
Index k maps to row k / columns and column k % columns.

approaches.name: Scan every cell
approaches.explanation: Compare every cell with the target.
approaches.tradeoff: No ordering assumption is needed, but the work is linear in cell count.
approaches.code: class Solution {public boolean searchMatrix(int[][] a,int t){for(int[] row:a)for(int x:row)if(x==t)return true;return false;}}

approaches.name: Virtual binary search
approaches.explanation: Binary-search flattened indices without copying cells. Long index arithmetic avoids multiplication overflow.
approaches.tradeoff: Requires global row-major ordering, not merely sorted rows and sorted columns.

search-a-2d-matrix.followup: How would you search when only rows and columns are individually sorted?

group-anagrams.statement: Group words with identical character multiplicities. Group order is arbitrary. The frequency approach assumes lowercase English letters.
group-anagrams.example: eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat → {eat,tea,ate}, {tan,nat}, {bat}.
hints: Anagrams share a canonical signature.
Sort the characters or count each letter.

approaches.name: Sorted signature
approaches.space: O(n × k) including output and keys
approaches.explanation: Sort a copy of each word to construct its map key. Anagrams produce the same key.
approaches.tradeoff: Supports more characters than a fixed 26-letter signature, but sorts every word.

approaches.name: Frequency signature
approaches.explanation: Count letter frequencies and serialize the vector with separators. Identical vectors identify anagrams.
approaches.tradeoff: Fast for long lowercase words. Unicode needs a normalization and counting policy.

group-anagrams.followup: Why are separators needed in frequency keys? How would Unicode normalization affect grouping?

subarray-sum-equals-k.statement: Count nonempty contiguous subarrays summing to k. Values may be negative. Assume sums and the count fit in int for the given constraints.
hints: A subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums.
Count earlier prefixes equal to currentPrefix-k.

approaches.name: Extend from each start
approaches.explanation: For each start, extend the end and maintain a running sum. Count every match.
approaches.tradeoff: Simple reference implementation. Negative numbers prevent safe early stopping.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int subarraySum(int[] a,int k){int count=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){int sum=0;for(int j=i;j<a.length;j++){sum+=a[j];if(sum==k)count++;}}return count;}}

approaches.name: Prefix frequencies
approaches.explanation: Seed prefix 0 with one occurrence. For each current prefix, count earlier prefixes with difference k before recording this prefix.
approaches.tradeoff: Extra space buys linear expected time. Sliding windows do not solve arbitrary negative-valued inputs.

subarray-sum-equals-k.followup: Why use frequencies rather than a set? Why record the current prefix after counting?

coin-change.statement: Find the fewest positive-denomination coins totaling a nonnegative amount. Coins can be reused. Return -1 if impossible.
hints: Let dp[x] mean the fewest coins for amount x.
Try every possible last coin.

approaches.name: Bottom-up dynamic programming
approaches.explanation: Set dp[0]=0 and all other entries to an unreachable sentinel. For every amount x, minimize 1+dp[x-coin] over coins that fit.
approaches.tradeoff: Pseudo-polynomial in the numeric amount. Memoized recursion has the same state bound but can overflow the call stack. Greedy is not generally correct.

coin-change.followup: How would you reconstruct chosen coins? Why must denominations be positive?

house-robber.statement: Maximize the sum of nonadjacent houses with nonnegative values. Return 0 for an empty street.
hints: Either skip the current house, or take it and skip the previous one.
Only two previous best totals are needed.

approaches.name: DP table
approaches.explanation: For every prefix, compare skipping its last house against taking that house plus the best total two houses earlier.
approaches.tradeoff: Retaining the table helps reconstruct chosen indices.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int rob(int[] a){int[] d=new int[a.length+2];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)d[i+2]=Math.max(d[i+1],d[i]+a[i]);return d[a.length+1];}}

approaches.name: Rolling state
approaches.explanation: Store just the two previous totals. Compute next before shifting the previous values.
approaches.tradeoff: Best when only the total is needed. Reconstructing selections requires more information.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int rob(int[] a){int p2=0,p1=0;for(int x:a){int next=Math.max(p1,p2+x);p2=p1;p1=next;}return p1;}}

house-robber.followup: How does a circular street change the solution?
house-robber.test: Solution s=new Solution();check(s.rob(new int[]{2,7,9,3,1})==12);check(s.rob(new int[]{})==0);check(s.rob(new int[]{5})==5);

product-of-array-except-itself.statement: Return the product of all other elements for every index without division. Assume prefix and suffix products fit in int.
hints: Split each product into values on the left and right.
Store left products in output; carry the right product in one variable.

approaches.name: Recompute products
approaches.explanation: For each index, multiply every other element.
approaches.tradeoff: Easy correctness baseline, but repeats multiplication.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int[] productExceptSelf(int[] a){int[] out=new int[a.length];for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){out[i]=1;for(int j=0;j<a.length;j++)if(i!=j)out[i]*=a[j];}return out;}}

approaches.name: Prefix and suffix
approaches.explanation: The forward pass stores the product strictly before each index. The reverse pass multiplies by the product strictly after it.
approaches.tradeoff: Handles zeros automatically and needs no division.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int[] productExceptSelf(int[] a){int[] out=new int[a.length];int p=1;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){out[i]=p;p*=a[i];}int s=1;for(int i=a.length-1;i>=0;i--){out[i]*=s;s*=a[i];}return out;}}

product-of-array-except-itself.followup: Why do two zeros work naturally? What if products exceed 64-bit range?

sort-colors.statement: Sort an array containing only 0, 1 and 2 in place.
hints: Count each of the three values for a simple two-pass method.
For one pass, maintain zero, one, unknown and two regions.

approaches.name: Count and rewrite
approaches.explanation: Count each value and then overwrite the array in ascending order.
approaches.tradeoff: Two passes but a very simple implementation.
approaches.code: class Solution {public void sortColors(int[] a){int[] c=new int[3];for(int x:a)c[x]++;int p=0;for(int x=0;x<3;x++)for(int k=0;k<c[x];k++)a[p++]=x;}}

approaches.name: Dutch national flag
approaches.explanation: Move zeroes left and twos right. After swapping with the right edge, inspect the incoming unknown value before advancing.
approaches.tradeoff: One pass with more delicate pointer invariants.
approaches.code: class Solution {public void sortColors(int[] a){int l=0,m=0,h=a.length-1;while(m<=h){if(a[m]==0){int t=a[l];a[l++]=a[m];a[m++]=t;}else if(a[m]==2){int t=a[h];a[h--]=a[m];a[m]=t;}else m++;}}}

sort-colors.followup: Why should mid not advance after swapping with high?

container-with-most-water.statement: Choose two nonnegative vertical heights to maximize their distance times the shorter height.
hints: The shorter edge limits the area.
A narrower pair retaining that shorter edge cannot improve on the current pair.

approaches.name: Every pair
approaches.explanation: Evaluate all left and right boundary pairs.
approaches.tradeoff: Useful reference for testing.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int maxArea(int[] a){int best=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<a.length;j++)best=Math.max(best,Math.min(a[i],a[j])*(j-i));return best;}}

approaches.name: Two pointers
approaches.explanation: Start at maximum width. Record area and move a pointer at the shorter edge. This eliminates only pairs dominated by one already examined.
approaches.tradeoff: Requires explaining the dominance proof, not merely memorizing the pointer rule.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int maxArea(int[] a){int l=0,r=a.length-1,best=0;while(l<r){best=Math.max(best,Math.min(a[l],a[r])*(r-l));if(a[l]<=a[r])l++;else r--;}return best;}}

container-with-most-water.followup: Prove why moving the shorter side is safe. When should area be long?

reverse-linked-list.statement: Reverse a singly linked list. Nodes have int val and ListNode next. Return the new head.
hints: Save the next node before overwriting its pointer.
Maintain a reversed prefix and untouched suffix.

approaches.name: Iterative reversal
approaches.explanation: Save next, point the current node backward, then advance prev and current.
approaches.tradeoff: Avoids recursion depth limits and reuses nodes.
approaches.code: class Solution {public ListNode reverseList(ListNode head){ListNode prev=null;while(head!=null){ListNode next=head.next;head.next=prev;prev=head;head=next;}return prev;}}

approaches.name: Recursive reversal
approaches.explanation: Reverse the suffix, point the successor back to this node, and clear this node’s forward pointer.
approaches.tradeoff: Compact, but long lists risk StackOverflowError in Java.
approaches.code: class Solution {public ListNode reverseList(ListNode h){if(h==null||h.next==null)return h;ListNode first=reverseList(h.next);h.next.next=h;h.next=null;return first;}}

reverse-linked-list.followup: Why must h.next be cleared? How would you reverse only a subrange?
reverse-linked-list.test: ListNode h=new ListNode(1);h.next=new ListNode(2);h.next.next=new ListNode(3);ListNode r=new Solution().reverseList(h);check(r.val==3&&r.next.val==2&&r.next.next.val==1&&r.next.next.next==null);check(new Solution().reverseList(null)==null);

validate-binary-search-tree.statement: Check strict BST ordering across all descendants. Duplicate keys are invalid.
validate-binary-search-tree.example: Root 5, right child 7, and 7’s left child 4 is invalid.
hints: Checking immediate children misses ancestor violations.
Carry an exclusive lower and upper bound.

approaches.name: Recursive bounds
approaches.explanation: Propagate allowable ranges from ancestors. Use long limits so all int node values can be represented.
approaches.tradeoff: Clear invariant, but a skewed tree can exhaust the call stack.
approaches.code: class Solution {public boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root){return valid(root,Long.MIN_VALUE,Long.MAX_VALUE);}private boolean valid(TreeNode n,long lo,long hi){return n==null||(lo<n.val&&n.val<hi&&valid(n.left,lo,n.val)&&valid(n.right,n.val,hi));}}

approaches.name: Iterative inorder
approaches.explanation: Inorder traversal of a strict BST must increase at every step. Reject any value no greater than the previous one.
approaches.tradeoff: Avoids recursive call-stack overflow.
approaches.code: class Solution {public boolean isValidBST(TreeNode n){java.util.Deque<TreeNode> s=new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();long prev=Long.MIN_VALUE;while(n!=null||!s.isEmpty()){while(n!=null){s.push(n);n=n.left;}n=s.pop();if(n.val<=prev)return false;prev=n.val;n=n.right;}return true;}}

validate-binary-search-tree.followup: What changes if duplicates are allowed only in right subtrees?
validate-binary-search-tree.test: TreeNode r=new TreeNode(5);r.left=new TreeNode(3);r.right=new TreeNode(7);check(new Solution().isValidBST(r));r.right.left=new TreeNode(4);check(!new Solution().isValidBST(r));check(new Solution().isValidBST(new TreeNode(Integer.MIN_VALUE)));

number-of-islands.statement: Count groups of land (character 1) in a rectangular grid using horizontal and vertical connectivity.
hints: Every unvisited land cell starts a new island.
Mark cells when enqueueing, not when dequeueing.

approaches.name: Iterative flood fill
approaches.explanation: Scan for land, count a new component, then erase every connected land cell using a queue. Mark before enqueueing so cells are visited once.
approaches.tradeoff: Mutates the grid. Preserve input using a copy or visited matrix. Recursive DFS has the same worst-case space but risks stack overflow.

number-of-islands.followup: Why might union-find be preferable when land is added incrementally?

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.statement: Find the longest contiguous substring without repeated characters. These versions treat Java UTF-16 char units as characters.
hints: Maintain a window containing unique characters.
Jump the left edge past the previous occurrence, but never move it backward.

approaches.name: Expand every start
approaches.explanation: Start a fresh set at each index and extend until encountering a duplicate.
approaches.tradeoff: Simple, but repeats work between overlapping windows.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s){int best=0;for(int i=0;i<s.length();i++){java.util.Set<Character> seen=new java.util.HashSet<>();for(int j=i;j<s.length()&&seen.add(s.charAt(j));j++)best=Math.max(best,j-i+1);}return best;}}

approaches.name: Last-seen window
approaches.explanation: For each right edge, update left to max(left,lastSeen+1). Record the new position and current window length.
approaches.tradeoff: Full Unicode code points or graphemes require a different segmentation policy.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s){java.util.Map<Character,Integer> last=new java.util.HashMap<>();int l=0,best=0;for(int r=0;r<s.length();r++){char c=s.charAt(r);l=Math.max(l,last.getOrDefault(c,-1)+1);last.put(c,r);best=Math.max(best,r-l+1);}return best;}}

longest-substring-without-repeating-char.followup: Trace abba to explain why max is necessary. How would you return the actual substring?

daily-temperatures.statement: For every temperature return days until a strictly warmer day, or 0 if none follows.
hints: A warm day can resolve many prior days.
Store unresolved indices in nonincreasing temperature order.

approaches.name: Forward search
approaches.explanation: Search forward from each day and stop at the first greater value.
approaches.tradeoff: Decreasing inputs trigger quadratic work.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] t){int[] a=new int[t.length];for(int i=0;i<t.length;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<t.length;j++)if(t[j]>t[i]){a[i]=j-i;break;}return a;}}

approaches.name: Monotonic stack
approaches.explanation: Pop every unresolved day colder than today and assign its distance. Every index is pushed and popped at most once.
approaches.tradeoff: Requires extra memory. Equal temperatures must remain unresolved.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] t){int[] out=new int[t.length];java.util.Deque<Integer> s=new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();for(int i=0;i<t.length;i++){while(!s.isEmpty()&&t[i]>t[s.peek()]){int j=s.pop();out[j]=i-j;}s.push(i);}return out;}}

daily-temperatures.followup: Why is the comparison strict? How would a circular sequence change the traversal?
daily-temperatures.test: check(java.util.Arrays.equals(new Solution().dailyTemperatures(new int[]{73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73}),new int[]{1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0}));check(java.util.Arrays.equals(new Solution().dailyTemperatures(new int[]{70,70}),new int[]{0,0}));

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.statement: Maximize profit with at most one buy followed by one sell. Return zero if no profitable trade exists.
hints: For each sell day, only the cheapest earlier buy matters.
Track a running minimum and best profit.

approaches.name: All buy/sell pairs
approaches.explanation: Enumerate every legal pair of buy before sell.
approaches.tradeoff: Useful as a test reference but repeats comparisons.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int maxProfit(int[] p){int best=0;for(int i=0;i<p.length;i++)for(int j=i+1;j<p.length;j++)best=Math.max(best,p[j]-p[i]);return best;}}

approaches.name: Running minimum
approaches.explanation: Update the lowest price seen and compare each price with it. Starting the best profit at zero naturally allows no trade.
approaches.tradeoff: Only handles a single transaction; cooldown and multi-transaction variants need more states.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int maxProfit(int[] p){int min=Integer.MAX_VALUE,best=0;for(int x:p){min=Math.min(min,x);best=Math.max(best,x-min);}return best;}}

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.followup: What changes with multiple transactions or a cooldown after selling?

valid-parenthesis.statement: Validate nesting of (), [], and {} brackets. Input contains only these bracket characters.
hints: The most recent unmatched opener must close first.
Push the expected closing bracket.

approaches.name: Expected closing stack
approaches.explanation: Opening brackets push their expected closer. A closing bracket must match the stack top. The stack must be empty at the end.
approaches.tradeoff: A single counter can handle one bracket kind but cannot enforce mixed nesting.
approaches.code: class Solution {public boolean isValid(String s){java.util.Deque<Character> st=new java.util.ArrayDeque<>();for(char c:s.toCharArray()){if(c=='(')st.push(')');else if(c=='[')st.push(']');else if(c=='{')st.push('}');else if(st.isEmpty()||st.pop()!=c)return false;}return st.isEmpty();}}

valid-parenthesis.followup: Why are equal counts not enough? How would quoted strings complicate parsing?

longest-increasing-subsequence.statement: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence; elements need not be adjacent.
hints: DP can compare a value to all earlier smaller values.
Retain the smallest possible tail for every subsequence length.

approaches.name: DP over endpoints
approaches.explanation: dp[i] is the best subsequence ending at i. Extend any earlier smaller value and retain the best length.
approaches.tradeoff: Easy to augment with predecessor pointers for reconstruction.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int lengthOfLIS(int[] a){int[] d=new int[a.length];int best=0;for(int i=0;i<a.length;i++){d[i]=1;for(int j=0;j<i;j++)if(a[j]<a[i])d[i]=Math.max(d[i],d[j]+1);best=Math.max(best,d[i]);}return best;}}

approaches.name: Minimum tails
approaches.explanation: Binary-search the first tail greater than or equal to the current value. Replace it, or append when every tail is smaller.
approaches.tradeoff: The tails array itself is not necessarily one valid subsequence. Reconstruction needs indices and predecessor links.
approaches.code: class Solution {public int lengthOfLIS(int[] a){int[] tails=new int[a.length];int size=0;for(int x:a){int l=0,r=size;while(l<r){int m=l+(r-l)/2;if(tails[m]<x)l=m+1;else r=m;}tails[l]=x;if(l==size)size++;}return size;}}

longest-increasing-subsequence.followup: Why replace the first greater-or-equal tail? How does a nondecreasing subsequence differ?

course-schedule.statement: Given courses and [course, prerequisite] pairs, determine whether all courses can be completed.
hints: A directed cycle makes the ordering impossible.
Repeatedly complete courses with no remaining prerequisites.

approaches.name: Topological processing
approaches.explanation: Build prerequisite-to-course edges and indegree counts. Completing a zero-indegree course decrements dependent indegrees. All courses are possible exactly when all are processed.
approaches.tradeoff: Iterative and can return an order. DFS with color states is another O(V+E) method but needs a traversal stack.

course-schedule.followup: How would you return a valid order or show the user an actual cycle?
